title: "abstract"
---



Dementia develops over decades but still lacks reliable markers of its onset and progression. DNA methylation reflects the gene regulation that changes with disease; despite numerous epigenome-wide studies, how methylation profiles evolve across the dementia continuum within a single population remains unclear. We profiled baseline blood methylation in 2,491 participants of the Age, Gene/Environment Susceptibility-Reykjavik Study (AGES-Reykjavik), followed up to 13.4 years and categorized into six clinically defined stages: stable normal cognition, two mild cognitive impairment (MCI) trajectories, two prospective transitions to dementia, and prevalent dementia. Relative to stable normal cognition, 403 CpG sites reached genome-wide significance in at least one stage, and dimensionality reduction recovered a continuous epigenetic trajectory paralleling clinical progression. Among participants cognitively normal at baseline, those who later developed dementia already carried dementia-concordant methylation, whereas those who progressed only to MCI carried the opposite. The same dimensions, learned without genotype data, ordered APOE risk groups in that direction, and effect sizes were concordant with independent Alzheimer's disease cohorts. Gene ontology showed stage-specific biology: synaptic, extracellular matrix and immune processes at the earliest transition, hypoxia response in stable MCI, and cell-cycle regulation in prevalent dementia. Blood methylation therefore resolves trajectory-specific change years before diagnosis, with early and late stages engaging distinct biology relevant to stage-appropriate risk stratification.
